---
title: "Collected Thoughts"
date: 2020-05-05
---

## Intention and expectation

Intention describes what I choose to do. Expectation describes what I think should happen in return. They often travel together, but I control the first more than the second.

Confusing them turns every action into a wager whose emotional payoff depends on circumstances I do not control.

## Validation

Wanting acknowledgment is not a flaw. We are social animals; inclusion matters. The problem begins when external approval becomes the only measurement that counts.

Awareness does not remove the desire for validation. It makes the dependency visible.

## Watching the mind

Thoughts appear, associate, and disappear, often without instruction. Observing that process changes my relation to it. A thought can be present without becoming an order, a belief, or an identity.

That small gap is easy to miss. It may be the beginning of choice.

## Experience as evidence

Some questions cannot be answered from a distance. Curiosity about travel is better tested by traveling. Curiosity about meditation is better tested by sitting still for a day.

Direct experience supplies data that thought alone cannot. It is evidence, not a conclusion.

## Impermanence

Almost none of my body or mental content is the same as it was a decade ago. Memory stitches these changing states into a continuous self.

Continuity need not be an illusion to be a construction. Seeing how it is built loosens the need to defend every current belief as a permanent part of me.

## Desire and happiness

Fulfilling a desire often produces satisfaction, but usually not for long. Another desire appears, or the new condition becomes ordinary.

This does not make desire bad. It means happiness cannot be modeled as a finite queue that, once cleared, leaves a permanent state. The system generates new items while processing the old ones.

Can joy exist without first requiring the world to change?

## Education

We measure education through information and skill because both are easy to test. Education could also expand attention, the ability to examine one's desires, and the capacity to disagree without treating disagreement as a threat.

Those outcomes are harder to measure, so they are easier to ignore.

## Identity

Beliefs compress experience into a usable model of the world and of myself. The model becomes a problem when new evidence feels like an attack.

A stable identity lowers the cost of everyday decisions. It can also raise the cost of changing my mind.

## Discipline

Discipline is repeated allocation of time toward a chosen direction. Its value is practical, not moral. A routine reduces the number of decisions between intention and action.

Small repetitions are difficult to evaluate because their effects appear later. That delay makes consistency easy to underestimate.

## Simplicity

When an experience becomes confusing, it helps to describe the facts before explaining them. What happened? What did I feel? What did I want? What am I afraid will happen next?

The story may still be necessary. It should come after observation, not replace it.

## Choosing a direction

Imagining an ideal day, work environment, relationship, or state of health is not prophecy. It produces constraints. A direction becomes useful only when it changes the next action.

Action then returns information and updates the model. Without that feedback, an ideal life can remain a collection of desires imported from other people.

## Anger

Anger narrows attention. One interpretation of events begins to feel complete, and alternatives disappear.

Observing the physical sensations may not end the anger, but it can reintroduce choice. The question is not whether awareness and anger can coexist. It is whether there is enough awareness to decide what happens next.
